extracted.intended_audience: students, practitioners, and general readers interested in Indian classical dance, drama, music, and aesthetic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on using Bharata Muni’s Rasa theory (Natya Shastra) to produce and evaluate performances that evoke specific audience emotions. Covers the bhava–rasa mechanism, the nine rasas with symbols, acting modalities, and musical mapping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasa as the essential purpose of art
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition or art of any kind cannot proceed without rasa; a vital task of the performer is to entice and inspire emotions in the viewer so that rasa connects performer and viewer with divinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat rasa as the primary objective of a performance — all elements (story, gesture, music) should aim to arouse an appropriate rasa. The article emphasizes that realising divinity can be achieved for the performer through performance and for the viewer by observation of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Rasa (emotional essence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasa (from Sanskrit meaning 'nectar' or 'taste') is the emotions and feelings that the audience experiences when witnessing art — the taste or essence the artwork imparts to the viewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning or evaluating a piece, identify the intended rasa (the emotional 'taste') and ensure the work's elements coherently produce that feeling in the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bhava as the performer's emotional states
rubrics_metrics.description: Bhava is the state of the mind — a mental disposition or attitude — and the bhavas of the performer are responsible for producing rasa in the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the performer’s inner states (bhavas) because these are the tools by which rasas are instigated; evaluate whether the performer’s bhavas are convincing and appropriate to the intended rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sthayi Bhava (dominant/permanent emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sthayi Bhava is the permanent or dominant emotion; when the sthayi together with Vibhava, Anubhava, and Vyabhicaribhava unite, the resultant effect is attainment of rasa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a clear sthayi as the anchor emotion for a scene or piece; supporting determinants and manifestations should reinforce this stable affect to yield a coherent rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vibhavas (determinants/motivations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vibhavas are the motivations that include the storyline, the actors, and the stage that awaken the sthayi bhava.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use setting, plot circumstances, props, and interpersonal triggers deliberately to create the vibhavas that motivate the intended sthayi and thus lead the audience toward the rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anubhavas (manifestations/expressions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anubhavas are the manifestations of the actors’ feelings — the visible/audible outcomes of inner bhavas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate physical and vocal manifestations (gestures, facial expressions, vocal inflection) to confirm they credibly express the inner bhava and help generate the rasa in the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vyabhicaribhavas (transient/emergent sentiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vyabhicaribhavas are the transient sentiments — the fleeting emotions (e.g., joy, pain, jealousy) that accompany the dominant sthayi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate appropriate fleeting emotions to enrich and color the sthayi; ensure they do not dilute the dominant emotion but support the complexity required to evoke the rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sattvic (sattvika) bhavas (involuntary expressions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sattvic bhava refers to involuntary emotions or expressions (e.g., blushes, perspiration) that accompany genuine emotional experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subtle involuntary signs strengthen authenticity; performers should cultivate believable sattvic responses to make bhavas and resulting rasas convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bhava→Rasa relationship (sequence of evocation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The interplay is: vibhava (stimulus) evokes anubhava (manifestation) together with vyabhicaribhavas and sattvic bhavas, which transform the viewer’s sthayi bhava into rasa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or composing scenes, trace whether the stimulus, manifestation, transient emotions, and involuntary signs logically produce the intended rasa in the spectator (example given: appearance of a beautiful girl → vibhava → anubhava → vyabhicaribhava → rasa of love or separation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shringara Rasa (love/beauty/attraction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shringara: the rasa of love, beauty, attraction; sthayi bhava is love; affiliated with Lord Vishnu and color dark blue or green. It can portray romance and erotic desire and may transcend to the individual–divine relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express through gestures and situations of attraction; recognize Shringara as 'mother of all rasas' and allow scope to include subsidiary emotions (compassion, jealousy, anger). Use appropriate ragas (e.g., Yaman) and movements in dance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hasya Rasa (laughter/joy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hasya: the rasa of laughter and joy, evoked through humor and happiness; color white and deity Pramatha or Shiva. Often arises from Shringara.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comedic dressing, ornaments, timing, and physical/vocal comic expression to generate Hasya; ensure timing and context make the humor support the dominant sthayi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Karuna Rasa (sorrow/compassion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Karuna: the rasa of sorrow, grief, and compassion; color grey and associated deity Yama. Portrayed when a character experiences pain or loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray through dejected facial expressions and actions that elicit empathy; align musical and narrative elements (e.g., ragas like Bhairavi) to enhance the compassionate mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raudra Rasa (anger/fury)
rubrics_metrics.description: Raudra (Rudra) rasa: manifests rage, anger, wrath; color red and God Rudra. Topics include rape, jealousy, threats, abuse; physical signs include redness in eyes, biting of lips, restlessness (vyabhicaribhavas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use intense physicality, vocal force, and aggressive staging to evoke Raudra; transient expressive signs should support the dominant fury without lapsing into caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veera Rasa (heroism/bravery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Veera rasa: the emotion of bravery and heroism; yellow or saffron color and associated with Lord Indra. Expresses determination, energy, self-confidence; notable gestures include widening eyes and expanded nostrils. Three types: dana veera, daya veera, yudha veera.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey forceful posture, assured movement and vocal confidence; choose the subtype of veera appropriate to the character's moral context (donation, sympathy, battlefield courage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bhayanaka Rasa (fear/panic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bhayanaka rasa: expresses fear; color black and associated deity Kala (God of Time). Evokes panic or dread; performers show raised eyebrows, quivering eyes, frantic glances, flared nostrils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create suspenseful vibhavas and use abrupt or tense manifestations to elicit fear; keep physical signs consistent with genuine panic to move the audience toward Bhayanaka.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bhibhatsa Rasa (disgust/loathing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bhibhatsa rasa: manifests hatred and disgust; associated color blue and God Mahakala. Expressed by squeezing limbs, rolling eyes, spitting, and other signs of revulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray visceral physical gestures and facial contortions to produce disgust; ensure such signs are contextually justified so audience empathy shifts appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adbhuta Rasa (wonder/amazement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adbhuta rasa: feeling of wonder and amazement; associated color gold and deity Gandharva. Can be Divya Adbhuta (seeing the divine) or Anand Adbhuta (expression of joy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visual or narrative elements that inspire curiosity or awe; staging, lighting, and music should amplify the sense of marvel without breaking credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shantha (Santha) Rasa (peace/tranquility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shantha rasa: serenity, peace and ultimate joy/bliss, often linked to self-realization; color jasmine/white and associated with Lord Narayana. Generally considered the ninth rasa added later by Abhinavagupta.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate stillness, calm pacing, minimalistic expression and subtle sattvic signs to evoke deep tranquility; suitable for spiritual or reflective scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols and representations (colors, deities, nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each rasa is symbolized by specific colors, deities and natural elements which reflect its emotional nature (e.g., Shringara—green; Raudra—ruby red; Bhayanaka—black).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use color palettes, iconography, and symbolic references in costume, set, and lighting to reinforce the intended rasa, while avoiding superficial or contradictory symbolism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four types of acting (Angika, Vachika, Aharya, Sattvika)
rubrics_metrics.description: The four types of acting in Natya Shastra are Angika (physical gestures), Vachika (vocal expressions), Aharya (costume and makeup), and Sattvika (emotional/involuntary expressions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design performances so these four modalities work together: physical technique, voice, visual presentation and internal emotional truth must align to produce bhavas and, consequently, rasas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raga–Rasa mapping in music
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasas govern the mood of musical compositions; specific ragas are tied with individual rasas (example: Yaman raga often used to depict Shringara; Bhairavi evokes Karuna).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or selecting music for a performance, choose ragas whose traditional emotive associations align with the intended rasa to strengthen audience affect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporary and cross-cultural application
rubrics_metrics.description: Though originating in ancient Indian performing arts, rasas are still used in modern performances (Bollywood, theatre, dance) and have been adapted by some Western playwrights/directors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply rasa principles flexibly across media and contemporary contexts, keeping the codified intent (evoking a specific rasa through bhavas and supporting elements) while adapting taste, pacing, and symbols for modern audiences.
